155.title: Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom day
155.hook: remembered each year, he is often called the shield of India
155.howItsDone: Sikhs mark Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom each year in late autumn with kirtan, readings and langar; many visit Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Delhi, where he was executed, and Gurdwara Rakab Ganj, where his body was cremated.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shaheed, and two small boys at Sirhind who would not bend. Your line was small, and unbending. Today, another martyr, and a shelter for strangers.

Strangers arrive at your door. They aren't your people, and they don't share your faith. They've traveled a long way, and they're frightened. Our families are being pressured to give up our religion, they say, and we don't know who else to ask. What would you say? Sikhs remember that this is what happened at Anandpur in 1675. The visitors were Kashmiri Pandits, Hindu scholars and priests. The man they came to see was the ninth Guru.
screen: `STRANGERS AT THE DOOR.` → `NOT YOUR FAITH, NOT YOUR PEOPLE.` → `WHAT WOULD YOU SAY?`

segments.voice: Guru Tegh Bahadur listened. Tradition says he sat quiet a long time, then said it would take the sacrifice of a great soul. His son Gobind, about nine years old, answered: who could be greater than you? So the Guru sent the Pandits back with a message for the officials of the emperor Aurangzeb: if Tegh Bahadur can be made to change his faith, we will all change ours. Then he set out for Delhi himself. He was arrested. Three of his companions, Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das and Bhai Dayala, were put to death in front of him, tradition says, to break him. He didn't break. In November 1675, in the square at Chandni Chowk in Delhi, he was beheaded. Gurdwara Sis Ganj stands on the spot now. Sikhs hold on to this: he gave his life for other people's right to worship, a right he didn't need for himself. He didn't wear their sacred thread or their forehead mark. His son, Guru Gobind Singh, later wrote that his father protected their tilak and their thread, and gave his head but not his faith. So he is called Hind di Chadar. Hind is India. A chadar is a sheet, a covering, the cloth you'd put over someone to shelter them. The covering of India. His own verses in the Guru Granth Sahib say, in paraphrase, that the wise one frightens no one and is afraid of no one. Sikhs mark his martyrdom every year, in late autumn, with kirtan, and many visit Sis Ganj.
screen: `A PLEA FROM KASHMIR.` · `WHO COULD BE GREATER THAN YOU?` · `CHANDNI CHOWK, 1675.` · `CHADAR — A SHELTERING CLOTH.` · then, large: `HIND DI CHADAR.`

segments.voice: Think of people anywhere who can't practice their faith freely, or who are pushed to take on one they don't hold; no need to name a country, just let them be people: a family at dinner, a grandmother, a kid at school who hides what she believes. If you pray, pray for their freedom, in your own words or simply with Waheguru. If you don't, wish them room to believe as they choose, and to be left in peace.

Your line: a shield for others. He covered a faith that wasn't his own. Day one hundred fifty-five.

156.title: Camp 3 close: your rhythm
156.hook: seva, kirtan, langar, simran, a bani and a visit: now assemble a week
156.howItsDone: Sikhs keep a daily Nitnem of set prayers at dawn, dusk and night, do simran, and go to the gurdwara weekly for kirtan, langar and seva; the rhythm grows over years rather than all at once.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Tegh Bahadur and Sis Ganj: a life given for other people's faith. Your line was a shield for others. Today, camp three comes to a close.

Nobody does every practice every day. This camp opened with seva nobody saw, and on its second day put you to work on the shoes by your door. Since then you've listened to kirtan, eaten sitting in a row on the floor, breathed the Name, learned the daily prayers and walked, in your mind at least, into a gurdwara. Then a whole year of festivals, from Vaisakhi to yesterday. So today isn't a new practice. It's you, with a pen, building a week.
screen: `IT STARTED WITH SEVA AND SHOES.` → `SIXTY DAYS OF PRACTICES.` → `NOW, BUILD A WEEK.`

segments.voice: Here's what this camp gave you, in six parts. Seva: nishkam seva, service with no audience; daswandh, a tenth for others; and a warning about haumai, the ego that loves credit. Kirtan: raag, the mood; rahao, the pause; the sangat singing back. Langar: pangat, the same row on the floor. Simran: the Name on the breath, the amrit vela before dawn, the mala, bead by bead. The banis: Nitnem, from Japji Sahib to Rehras at dusk and Sohila at night. And the visit: the open door, matha tekna, the chaur, karah prashad, the hukamnama. Then the Sikh year: Vaisakhi, nagar kirtan, gurpurabs, akhand path, chhabeel, Bandi Chhor, Hola Mohalla, Maghi, shaheed, Sis Ganj. Sikhs have a word for a daily rule, and you've met it: Nitnem. Nit means daily; nem is a rule, a discipline you keep. In Sikh practice, faith isn't left to a mood that comes and goes. It's built into the day: early morning, evening, night. And into the week: the gurdwara, the langar, the sangat. The Sikh Rehat Maryada sets Nitnem as a daily discipline, and the gurdwara gives the week its shape. A rhythm holds you on the days motivation doesn't. It isn't a test. A small rhythm you keep will carry you further than a big one you drop by Thursday. For a learner or a partner it might be one bani, one meal shared, one quiet morning. Tomorrow a new camp begins: the text itself. Japji Sahib, line by line, starting with its alphabet.
screen: `SEVA, KIRTAN, LANGAR.` · `SIMRAN, THE BANIS, THE VISIT.` · `NITNEM — A DAILY RULE.` · `SMALL AND KEPT.` · then, large: `YOUR RHYTHM.`

segments.voice: Take a pen, or a note on your phone, and write seven short lines, one for each day of the week, each with one small thing from this camp: a bani, five minutes of simran, an unseen seva, one shabad, a meal shared, and a gurdwara day if one is near. Keep every line small enough that a bad day could still manage it, with Waheguru at the top if you pray. Then read your seven lines back once, slowly.
Nitnem. A daily rule, kept morning, evening and night: your own rhythm, sized to your life.
Your line: you can do this. Small and kept, the rhythm is yours now. Camp three, complete.

157.title: The Guru's alphabet
157.hook: Gurmukhi, from the Guru's mouth, has thirty-five letters and a set of vowel signs
157.howItsDone: Sikh children often learn the Gurmukhi letters at gurdwara Punjabi classes, reciting the painti aloud, so that they can read Gurbani for themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nitnem: a daily rule, small enough to keep, and camp three came to a close. Your line was you can do this.

Plastic letters on a fridge door. A for apple, B for ball. Before a child can read a single word, they can make the sounds, and they'll say them to anyone who'll listen. Today a new camp begins the same way, with letters. For the next seventy-five days, you and i will read one text together, slowly: Guru Nanak's Japji Sahib, the first hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib. First, the script it's written in.
screen: `MAGNETS ON THE FRIDGE.` → `A NEW CAMP: THE TEXT.` → `JAPJI SAHIB, LINE BY LINE.`

segments.voice: The script is Gurmukhi. Gur is Guru; mukhi comes from mukh, the mouth. From the mouth of the Guru. Sikhs trace it to Guru Angad, the second Guru, who, tradition says, shaped and settled the letters so the Sikhs could write down Guru Nanak's hymns. The letters grew out of older scripts already used in Punjab; Guru Angad gave them a form, and a purpose. The alphabet is called the painti, which simply means thirty-five, for its thirty-five basic letters. It opens with three letters that carry vowels, oora, aira and eeree, then the consonants march in neat rows: sassa, haha, then kakka, khakha, gagga, and on. Small vowel signs above, below and beside the letters change the sound. Later, a handful of extra letters with a dot at the foot were added for sounds borrowed from Persian, so modern charts show a few more than thirty-five. Here's the gift for a learner: Gurmukhi is close to phonetic. Mostly, you say what you see. So you can sound out Japji long before you understand it, the way a child sings a song before knowing what the words mean. And, as you saw on day nine, the very first character of the Guru Granth Sahib isn't a letter at all. It's the numeral one, joined to the letter oora, with a long curve sweeping over the top: Ik Onkar. The One, who is everywhere. The whole scripture begins with a number and a sound. So in this camp, read with the mouth first. Understanding follows.
screen: `GURMUKHI — FROM THE GURU'S MOUTH.` · `GURU ANGAD SETTLES THE LETTERS.` · `THE PAINTI — THIRTY-FIVE.` · `SAY WHAT YOU SEE.` · then, large: `IK ONKAR.`

segments.voice: Look at Ik Onkar on the screen, lift one finger, and trace it slowly in the air, as if writing on a window: the numeral one, the round letter beside it, then the long curve that sweeps up over the top and keeps going. Do it three times, a little smoother each time, saying Ik Onkar quietly if you pray. Then rest your hand in your lap, breathe, and let the shape stay behind your eyes.
Gurmukhi. From the Guru's mouth: the script of the Guru Granth Sahib, with thirty-five letters and a set of vowel signs.
Your line: read with the mouth first. Every letter starts as a sound. See you tomorrow.

158.title: Sound before meaning
158.hook: Japji is meant to be heard; we will listen to each pauri before we learn what it says
158.howItsDone: Sikhs recite or listen to Japji Sahib each morning, often from memory, as the first bani of Nitnem; children often hear it long before they study its meaning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gurmukhi, the script from the Guru's mouth, and Ik Onkar traced in the air. Your line was read with the mouth first. Today, why the sound comes first.

A lullaby in a language you don't speak can still get through. So can a chant in a stadium, or a hymn at a wedding where you catch one word in ten. The meaning never arrives. The sound does, and it stays. Japji often reaches people that way first. In homes where it's recited at dawn, children hear it drifting from a kitchen or a car radio long before anyone explains what it says.
screen: `A SONG YOU DON'T UNDERSTAND.` → `THE SOUND STAYED.` → `JAPJI AT DAWN, FROM THE KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: So this camp has a rule. Almost every pauri, every stanza, gets two days. Day one is sound: listen, and say the opening line out loud. Day two is meaning: what the Guru is saying. Why that order? Partly because of what Japji is. The name comes from jap, to recite, to repeat. It was made to be said, not only studied. It's the first bani of the morning Nitnem, often said from memory: thirty-eight pauris, with a short salok at the start and another at the end, and a steady recitation fits into an ordinary morning. Partly because of how Gurbani, the Guru's word, speaks about itself. The hymns keep praising the shabad, the word as sound, and the naad, the sound that moves through everything, as things that work on the one who hears them. Japji itself will give four whole pauris to one word: suniai, by listening. And partly it's simply how learning works. Understanding goes deeper when it lands on something familiar. If you've said a line thirty times, then on the day its meaning arrives, it has somewhere to sit. There's a humility in it, too. You don't have to understand everything before you start. And if you grew up Sikh and can't read Gurmukhi, or follow only some of the Punjabi in the hymns, you're in large company, especially far from Punjab. Some people carry a quiet embarrassment about that. There's no need. The Granth's language is centuries old, fluent speakers look words up too, and this camp is built for exactly where you are. When the meanings open, i'll follow Macauliffe's 1909 translation, retold in plain words. For now, the instruction is short. Listen.
screen: `TWO DAYS FOR EACH PAURI.` · `JAPJI IS MADE TO BE SAID.` · `THE SHABAD WORKS ON THE LISTENER.` · `LISTEN FIRST, UNDERSTAND LATER.` · then, large: `SOUND BEFORE MEANING.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and listen to whatever is around you, the hum of a fridge, traffic, a bird, your own breath, without naming the sounds. If you have a recording of Japji Sahib, and there are many, let it play and wash past you, without following the words or looking anything up. If you pray, simply sit inside it.
Japji Sahib. In this camp, each pauri of it is heard and said before it is explained, sound before meaning.
Your line: listen before you understand. The meaning can wait its turn. That's day one hundred fifty-eight.

159.title: The Mool Mantar, sounded
159.hook: Ik Onkar, Satnam, Karta Purakh, Nirbhau, Nirvair, Akal Murat, Ajuni, Saibhang, Gur Prasad
159.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the Mool Mantar at the start of Japji each morning and at many other moments; a short form, Ik Onkar Satgur Prasad, stands at the head of hymns throughout the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Japji Sahib, and this camp's rule: sound before meaning. Your line was listen before you understand. Today, the first sounds of all.

Every community has a line people know by heart, words that come out without thinking, at a wedding, a funeral, a bedside. Sikhs have one that comes before everything else. It opens the Guru Granth Sahib. It opens Japji. A short form of it stands at the head of hymns all through the scripture. It's the Mool Mantar, the root verse. Today, no explaining. Just how it sounds.
screen: `A LINE EVERYONE KNOWS.` → `IT OPENS THE WHOLE GRANTH.` → `TODAY, ONLY THE SOUND.`

segments.voice: Mool means root. Mantar is a verse to be repeated. The root verse. Here it is, slowly, in its pieces. Ik Onkar. Ik, like ick; Onkar, ong-KAAR. Sat Naam. Sat, rhyming with but; naam, like calm with an n. Kartaa Purakh. KAR-taa, PUR-akh. Nirbhau. nir-BHOW, like now, with a breath on the b. Nirvair. nir-VAIR, like air. Akaal Moorat. a-KAAL, MOO-rat. Ajoonee. a-JOO-nee. Saibhang. say-BHUNG. Gur Prasaad. gur pra-SAAD. That's the whole thing: fourteen short words, the way they're spaced here. Said slowly, it takes less than half a minute. You met some of their meanings back on days ten and eleven, and you'll keep meeting them all through Japji: one; truth is the name; the maker; without fear; without hate; beyond time; unborn; self-existent; known by the Guru's grace. Now notice the sound itself. It moves in short beats, two and three syllables at a time, easy to breathe with. Its first sound is a number: ik, one. Its middle is a run of nirs and a's, nirbhau, nirvair, akaal, ajoonee, each saying what the One is not: not afraid, not hating, not bound by time, not born. And the last two words, gur prasaad, turn the whole verse into a gift: not something you figure out, but something given. Sikhs differ a little on where the Mool Mantar ends. Some end it at gur prasaad. Others carry on through the next lines, to Naanak hosee bhee sach. Either way, every word of it is said each morning at the start of Japji.
screen: `MOOL — ROOT. MANTAR — VERSE.` · `SHORT BEATS, EASY TO BREATHE.` · `IT STARTS WITH A NUMBER.` · `GUR PRASAAD — A GIFT.` · then, large: `THE MOOL MANTAR.`

segments.voice: Sit up, breathe in, and say it slowly, out loud if you can, in a whisper if you can't, with a breath between each piece: Ik Onkar, Sat Naam, Kartaa Purakh, Nirbhau, Nirvair, Akaal Moorat, Ajoonee, Saibhang, Gur Prasaad. Then say it once more, a little smoother, without worrying about every vowel; say what you heard. If you pray, it's already a prayer; if you're learning, it's a sound worth knowing by heart.

160.title: The title word
160.hook: after the Mool Mantar comes one word, jap: recite, repeat, remember
160.howItsDone: Japji Sahib takes its name from jap, to recite and remember; Sikhs recite it each morning, and many also repeat Waheguru or the Mool Mantar through the day as simran.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mool Mantar, the root verse, from Ik Onkar to Gur Prasaad. Your line was sound it out. Today, one word on its own line.

One word on a sticky note on the bathroom mirror: call. Milk. Breathe. Not a sentence, because one word is all you need to remember by. Right after the Mool Mantar, before the first verse of Japji begins, a single word stands on its own line. Most people read straight past it. It's the title of the whole hymn. And it isn't really a name, the way a book title is. It's closer to a note on the mirror.
screen: `A STICKY NOTE ON THE MIRROR.` → `ONE WORD, ON ITS OWN LINE.` → `A TITLE LIKE A NOTE.`

segments.voice: The word is jap. In Gurmukhi it's just two letters, with a small vowel mark under the second that carries grammar and is mostly left silent. You've met its meaning before, folded inside a longer name: on day twenty-one and again on day one hundred twenty-nine, Japji Sahib, the recitation, with ji and sahib added for respect. Today, look at the word with the respect taken off, standing alone on its line. Across Indian religious life there's a practice called japa: repeating a sacred name or phrase, often on beads. You met the mala in camp three. Jap comes from the same root. So the bare title of Guru Nanak's great morning hymn reads like one instruction: repeat. Or: remember. But Japji itself will teach that it isn't asking for mechanical repetition. Much later in the hymn, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that if one tongue became a hundred thousand, and each repeated the Name a hundred thousand times, those would be the steps of a stairway toward the Lord. Repetition is a stairway. Yet the whole hymn insists the point is remembering, not counting: keeping the One in mind while you live. That's why jap sits so close to simran, remembrance, from camp three. Say something enough times and it stops being something you say and becomes something you know in your bones, like your own phone number, a friend's laugh, the way home in the dark. Jap asks for that kind of knowing. The stairway is made of small repetitions. Each one is only one step.
screen: `A ONE-WORD TITLE.` · `JAP — RECITE, REPEAT, REMEMBER.` · `THE TITLE, WITH THE RESPECT TAKEN OFF.` · `REPETITION IS A STAIRWAY.` · then, large: `JAP.`

segments.voice: On your next out-breath, whisper the word jap, then breathe in, three times over. Then stop and listen to the quiet after it, the way a room sounds after a bell, and notice what you'd like to remember today: a person, a promise, the One, if that's your language. If you pray, let Waheguru follow on the next breaths, and rest there.
Jap. Recite, repeat, remember: the one-word title of Guru Nanak's morning hymn.
Your line: repeat, remember. One word stood alone at the top of Japji today. A hundred and sixty days now.

161.title: Aad sach: the sound
161.hook: aad sach, jugaad sach, hai bhi sach, Nanak hosi bhi sach
161.howItsDone: The salok 'aad sach, jugaad sach' follows the Mool Mantar at the start of Japji; sangats also sing it as simple kirtan, repeating it many times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jap, the one-word title of Japji: recite, repeat, remember. Your line was repeat, remember.

Four little claims, and the same word landing at the end of each one, like a drum hitting the same beat four times. That's the shape of the short verse right after the title, jap: a salok, just two lines long. It's sung as well as recited. You'll hear it at the start of Japji every morning, and at gatherings as kirtan, sung round and round until the whole room is singing. You can feel its shape before you know a single word.
screen: `ONE WORD, FOUR TIMES.` → `A SALOK, TWO LINES LONG.` → `SUNG ROUND AND ROUND.`

segments.voice: Here it is, slowly. Aad sach. Jugaad sach. Hai bhee sach. Naanak hosee bhee sach. Listen for the word that keeps coming back: sach. It sounds a little like such, said softly. That's the drumbeat. Now the pieces. Aad: a long a, as in father. Jugaad: ju-GAAD, and inside it is jug, an age, a great stretch of time. Hai bhee: hai, like high, and bhee, like bee with a breath on the b. Naanak: the Guru's own name, NAA-nak. Hosee bhee: HO-see bhee. Now the shape. The first line is two short pairs: aad sach, jugaad sach. The second stretches out, three beats, then four, as if the verse leans forward. And hear what the pieces sound like before you know them: aad, a beginning; jug, the ages; hai, is; hosee, will be. It moves from before, through the long ages, to right now, and on into what's coming. In every line, the same word holds still while the time around it moves. The sound is teaching before the meaning arrives; what sach means, and what the four lines claim, comes tomorrow. In Gurmukhi, sach carries the same small silent mark under its last letter that you saw on jap. Sangats often sing this salok as simple kirtan, and with one word coming back four times, it's easy to join.
screen: `SACH — THE DRUMBEAT.` · `AAD, JUGAAD, HAI BHEE, HOSEE.` · `THE SECOND LINE STRETCHES.` · `ONE WORD HOLDS STILL.` · then, large: `AAD SACH.`

segments.voice: Say it four times, out loud if you can: aad sach, jugaad sach, hai bhee sach, Naanak hosee bhee sach. Each round a little slower and softer, letting sach land, until the last is almost a whisper. Then sit, let the last sach fade, and notice your breath went on the whole time underneath the words; if you pray, you can stay with Waheguru in the quiet.
